PLAs are characterized by their ability to converge to the optimal solution in specific problems, a trait that motivates their application in RL, traditionally dominated by the use of Deep Neural Networks (DNNs). By employing PLAs, researchers can potentially develop RL agents that are more interpretable and offer solutions to real-world problems in a more transparent manner. Furthermore, we investigate the convergence properties of this PLA-based RL agent and demonstrate its ability to converge in a reasonable timeframe, depending on the specific problem and the resources available. Additionally, we conduct an in-depth analysis of the learned representations to better understand their nature and potential for improving the efficiency of this PLA-based RL agent. 

The contributions of this study include the development of a novel RL agent that combines the convergence properties of PLA and the expressiveness of neural networks, an analysis of the convergence properties of this PLA-based RL agent, and an in-depth investigation into the representations learned by this PLA within the context of RL. We hope that this work will inspire future research into PLA-based RL methods. We anticipate that this new approach will be more suitable for certain applications, such as healthcare, where interpretability is crucial.

A key challenge in active learning is developing an efficient strategy for selecting the next data points that need labeling.  A straightforward yet effective strategy for addressing this challenge involves using an ensemble of models to make predictions and then selecting the data points that the individual models struggle with the most.  However, this approach can be time-consuming and may not work well with vast amounts of unlabeled data.  A more efficient alternative involves employing a random forest to make selections based on the predictions of multiple models.  A new method proposed in this paper uses a similar approach but makes a few significant improvements.  First, this method uses a dynamic forest that adapts to the available data.  Second, it uses a novel technique for prioritizing data points that takes into account both their predicted class and how well that prediction holds up across different models.  Experimental results demonstrate that this new method outperforms existing methods, particularly when there is a significant disparity in how accurately each class of data is predicted. We have developed a method for producing high-quality, indistinguishable single qubits in optical lattices, using a precise combination of microwave, optical, and light-shift control. This technique enables the creation of a broad range of two-dimensional lattices with a single photon per site, yielding extremely high qubit purity ($\sim93.5\%$), extremely high emitters' coherence times ($\sim1.1\,\mu$s) and a very low emitters' loss rate ($\sim10^{-4}\,\rm s^{-1}$). Moreover, we have demonstrated the ability to generate high-fidelity, controlled entangled states in two-dimensional lattices, with a high fidelity of approximately $0.89\%$. This breakthrough marks the first successful production of high-fidelity, controlled entangled states in large two-dimensional lattices with a single photon per site, opening the door to a wide range of quantum simulation, cryptography, and sensing applications. This achievement is expected to greatly enhance the capabilities of quantum computing and communication systems. For instance, it could be leveraged to rapidly develop quantum algorithms for simulating complex systems and performing optimized quantum measurements.
